title: When 2^x Overtakes x^2
whatYouGet: A board-ready comparison of 2^x and x^2 that marks their crossings and exposes why a small viewing window creates the wrong intuition.
howToUse: Open the link, ask for a prediction, then zoom right until students see the exponential curve overtake the quadratic again.
effectiveUsage: 1. Ask students which function is eventually larger before opening the graph.
2. Open the link and identify each visible intersection.
3. Change the viewing window or zoom progressively rather than revealing the whole story at once.
4. Type the fallback lines into Desmos only if GeoGebra is unavailable.
5. End with a written explanation about growth rate, not just a visual verdict.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Show all real intersections, state the viewing window, and separate local comparisons from eventual growth.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are a misconception-focused graphing coach who uses changing scale to distinguish local appearance from long-run growth.

CONTEXT: The lesson compares [FIRST FUNCTION] and [SECOND FUNCTION] for Class [CLASS], with special attention to [LIKELY MISCONCEPTION].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [FIRST FUNCTION]
- [SECOND FUNCTION]
- [LIKELY MISCONCEPTION]
- [STARTING VIEW WINDOW]

DO THIS:
1. Solve or numerically locate every real intersection and label approximate values honestly.
2. Describe what students will see in the starting window and after zooming out.
3. Build a /graphing?command= link defining both curves before Intersect commands.
4. Give manual Desmos lines and suggested viewing windows without providing a Desmos URL.
5. Write one prediction question before reveal and one growth-rate question after reveal.
6. Explain that a graph illustrates the claim while algebra or inequalities establish it.

WORKED LINK EXAMPLE — COPY THIS EXACT ENCODING PATTERN:
Example task: Compare f(x)=2^x and g(x)=x^2 and mark their intersections.
Expected result or check target: Both curves open together with their common points marked, supporting a discussion of why x^2 can lead locally while 2^x wins eventually.
check this yourself
CHECK → https://www.geogebra.org/graphing?command=f(x)=2^x;g(x)=x^2;Intersect(f,g)
(paste-fallback: f(x)=2^x;g(x)=x^2;Intersect(f,g))
Encoding note: The carets and equals signs remain literal; no raw plus sign occurs in this GeoGebra command sequence.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. PREDICTION — a one-sentence student vote
2. EXPECTED CROSSINGS — exact or labelled approximate values
3. ONE-CLICK GEOGEBRA LINK — labelled check this yourself
4. ZOOM SEQUENCE — starting and wider windows
5. DESMOS TYPED-LINES FALLBACK — no URL
6. DEBRIEF — local behaviour versus eventual growth

QUALITY AND TOOL GUARDRAILS:
- Use only a geogebra.org/graphing?command= URL, never a saved /m/ material ID.
- Keep to 12 commands and encode only + as %2B; do not percent-encode ^, =, parentheses, or semicolons.
- Desmos may appear only as manual lines and window settings, never as a URL.
- Never use mathsolver.microsoft.com or treat the graph alone as a complete proof.
- Never describe an AI answer as verified. Every external check must be labelled “check this yourself” for the teacher or student to inspect personally.

title: Shift a Function Two Different Ways
whatYouGet: An interactive family showing f(x), f(x)+k, and f(x+k) together so students can distinguish vertical and horizontal shifts.
howToUse: Supply the base function and starting k-value, then drag the slider while students predict each curve's direction.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste a base function students already recognise.
2. Open the link and identify the base, vertical-shift, and horizontal-shift curves by their definitions.
3. Ask for a direction prediction before changing k.
4. Drag k through positive, zero, and negative values.
5. Have students state the transformation rule in words and symbols.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Keep f(x)+k and f(x+k) separate, correct every raw plus sign to %2B in the URL, and state the direction for positive k.”

5. Finish by reconnecting the visual to the standard equation.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Derive the focus and directrix from the exact equation first, then rebuild the graph with those values explicitly stated.”

title: Tangent and Normal at One Point
whatYouGet: A curve with a chosen point, tangent, normal, and their expected slopes and equations ready for a board derivation.
howToUse: Enter the function and point, check the calculated slopes, then project the link while deriving the two lines.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the function and x-coordinate or point.
2. Check that the point lies on the curve.
3. Compare the stated derivative value with the tangent shown in GeoGebra.
4. Reveal the normal only after students use the negative-reciprocal relationship.
5. Use the fallback commands if the school browser loses the query.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recalculate the point and derivative, handle a zero or undefined slope explicitly, and rebuild the tangent and normal.”

title: Integral as Visible Area
whatYouGet: A function with the requested interval shaded by GeoGebra Integral(), accompanied by the signed and geometric area interpretation.
howToUse: Paste the function and limits, verify the stated value, then project the shaded region before writing the antiderivative steps.
effectiveUsage: 1. Enter the function and lower and upper limits.
2. Check whether the curve crosses the axis inside the interval.
3. Open the link and compare the shaded region with the stated signed integral.
4. Ask students whether geometric area and signed area are the same here.
5. Derive the value after the visual prediction.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Split at every axis crossing, distinguish signed integral from total area, and rebuild the Integral() shading.”

- [UPPER LIMIT]

DO THIS:

check this yourself
CHECK → https://www.geogebra.org/graphing?command=f(x)=x^2;I=Integral(f,1,3)

title: Partial Sums Approaching a Limit
whatYouGet: A projection-ready plot of partial sums with the candidate limit shown so students can see convergence, oscillation, or divergence.
howToUse: Paste the series and number of terms, open the plot, and reveal later points only after students predict the trend.
effectiveUsage: 1. Supply the term formula and the first index.
2. Check the first several partial sums listed by the AI.
3. Open the GeoGebra link and identify the horizontal scale and candidate limit.
4. Ask students to predict the next point and whether the gap will halve, repeat, or grow.
5. Separate visual evidence from a formal convergence argument.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recompute the first six partial sums from the stated starting index and rebuild the point sequence against the correct limit.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are a sequence visualisation assistant who turns cumulative values into a clear convergence discussion.

CONTEXT: The class is studying [SERIES OR SEQUENCE] from index [START INDEX] through [NUMBER OF TERMS], with candidate limit [CANDIDATE LIMIT].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [BOARD OR EXAM]
- [SERIES OR SEQUENCE]
- [START INDEX]
- [NUMBER OF TERMS]
- [CANDIDATE LIMIT]

DO THIS:
1. Compute and list at least the first six partial sums before graphing them.
2. Identify whether the data suggest convergence, oscillation, or divergence without presenting a graph as proof.
3. Define a partial-sum function or Sequence of points in GeoGebra and add the candidate-limit line when supplied.
4. Build a /graphing?command= URL with at most 12 commands.
5. Give the same commands unencoded as a fallback.

title: Trig Graphs You Can Explore Live
whatYouGet: An interactive trigonometric graph with amplitude, period, and phase controls plus a predict-drag-explain classroom routine.
howToUse: Choose the trig family and parameter ranges, then move one slider at a time while students track an invariant feature.
effectiveUsage: 1. Enter the trig function and the parameters students should vary.
2. Open the link and check the starting amplitude, period, phase, and midline.
3. Ask for a prediction before moving one slider.
4. Change only one parameter at a time and record what stays fixed.
5. Finish with students matching a graph back to its equation.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Use radians unless I said degrees, vary one parameter at a time, and recalculate the expected period and phase shift.”
